title: Nvidia chips pile up in Hong Kong as China withholds import approval
author: B
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

The story is about China’s desire to build AI clashing with its desire to reduce dependence on American technology.

Reuters reports that roughly 600,000 Nvidia H200 AI chips are sitting in Hong Kong, waiting to enter mainland China because Beijing hasn’t approved large-scale imports—even though Chinese tech companies want them. Some smaller shipments have been allowed through. ca.finance.yahoo.com

Why the holdup? Beijing wants companies to use Chinese chips, but Nvidia’s hardware and software remain especially useful for training AI models. The U.S. has permitted H200 sales to approved Chinese customers, so China’s own import restrictions are now another obstacle. Limited supply has also pushed up unofficial-market prices. ca.finance.yahoo.com

It matters because access to these chips affects how quickly Chinese companies can develop AI—and who supplies the technology behind it.

For China’s AI companies: delayed deliveries mean less computing power to train models, potentially slowing development and raising costs.
For Beijing: restricting imports can encourage domestic chipmakers, but it also limits Chinese companies’ access to hardware they want today.
For Nvidia: strong demand doesn’t automatically become sales when both U.S. export rules and Chinese import approvals control access. Reuters reports about 600,000 H200 chips waiting in Hong Kong. ca.finance.yahoo.com
The broader significance is that AI competition increasingly depends on government decisions as well as better technology. These chips are caught between China’s immediate AI ambitions and its longer-term goal of technological independence.

The takeaway: the chips and demand exist, but government policy is keeping them apart. China faces a tradeoff between getting computing power now and developing a more independent domestic chip industry.
